content: Glucagon is a hormone that is naturally produced in the pancreas. It is prescribed to treat severe hypoglycemia (very low blood sugar levels). Additionally, glucagon is sometimes used during diagnostic procedures involving the stomach and other digestive organs. In some cases, it may be prescribed for other purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Glucagon is typically administered via injection under the skin, into a muscle, or directly into a vein. It is supplied as a powder and a liquid, which must be mixed immediately before use. Detailed instructions for mixing and administering the injection are included in the medication package. Glucagon should be given as soon as possible after identifying that the patient is unconscious due to low blood sugar. After administering the injection, the patient should be turned onto their side to prevent choking in case of vomiting. Once glucagon has been administered, contact your doctor promptly. It is crucial for all patients to have a household member who is familiar with the symptoms of low blood sugar and knows how to administer glucagon. If you frequently experience low blood sugar, always carry a glucagon kit with you. Symptoms of low blood sugar include shakiness, dizziness, lightheadedness, sweating, confusion, nervousness, irritability, sudden behavioral or mood changes, headache, numbness or tingling around the mouth, weakness, pale skin, sudden hunger, and clumsy or jerky movements. If possible, consume a food or beverage containing sugar, such as hard candy or fruit juice, before glucagon administration becomes necessary. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist to clarify any part you or your household members do not understand. Use glucagon exactly as directed. Do not use more or less of it, or take it more frequently than prescribed by your doctor. Before using glucagon, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to glucagon, any other medications, or beef or pork products. Additionally, disclose all prescription and nonprescription medications, including vitamins, that you are currently taking. Notify your doctor if you have a history of adrenal gland problems, blood vessel disease, malnutrition, pancreatic tumors, insulinoma, or pheochromocytoma. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Glucagon may cause side effects. Minor side effects include an upset stomach, vomiting, rash, or itching. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Severe side effects, such as difficulty breathing or loss of consciousness, require immediate medical attention. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store glucagon in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture (do not store it in the bathroom). Once the injection dose has been mixed, discard any unused portion. In case of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Do not share your medication with anyone else. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist.
